subtitle.latin: Tarpeia rupes prope est Capitolinum montem
subtitle.english: The Tarpeian Rock is near the Capitol

latin: — Huc accedite. Hinc prospectus late patet<sup>1</sup>.
— Non credebam urbem tam latam esse. Quod flumen hoc est?
— Tiberis<sup>2</sup> urbem in partes duas dividit et usque ad portum Ostiensem fluit.
— Et prope nos, hi horti cum lacu medio<sup>3</sup>?
— Sunt horti Caesariani. Lacus ad naumachias<sup>4</sup> exhibendas a Caesare Augusto effossus est.
— Pone eos vides Pontem Sublicium qui olim sublicis<sup>5</sup> innitebatur.
— Trans Tiberim, collis<sup>6</sup> hic proximus est mons Capitolinus, cum templo Jovis<sup>7</sup> Optimi Maximi ad sinistram et Rupe<sup>8</sup> Tarpeia ad dextram.
— Cur dicunt Rupem Tarpeiam prope Capitolinum montem esse?
— Quia viri clarissimi triumphantes in clivum<sup>9</sup> Capitolinum ascendebant, sed rei publicae proditores<sup>10</sup> e Rupe Tarpeia, quae proxima est, praecipitabantur.
— Nonnunquam iidem erant et brevis erat via ab honoribus ad supplicium!
— Haec moles<sup>11</sup> quae in ripa dextra Tiberis apparet, nonne Hadriani<sup>12</sup> Mausoleum<sup>13</sup> est?
— Ita, et ad dextram Vaticanus mons cum Petriana<sup>14</sup> Basilica<sup>15</sup>.
— Cras Civitatem Vaticanam visitabimus et fortasse Summum Pontificem videbimus.
— Ubi est forum?
— Id non videmus, nam Capitolino monte occultatur, sed a summo Capitolino monte longe lateque aspicitur.
— Hic pons ferriviarius quem ad orientem videmus, pyrobolisne<sup>16</sup> aeriis destructus est?
— Proh! Omnino erras. Perendie tibi documentum de illa quaestione legendum praebebo.
english: — Come up here! From here the view [is very open] (widely extends).
— I didn't think the city was so big. What is this river?
— The Tiber divides the city into two parts and flows as far as the port of Ostia.
— And near us, these gardens with a lake in the middle?
— They are Caesar's Gardens. The lake was dug by (Caesar) Augustus for [mock naval battles] (to show).
— [Behind] (pone, adv.) them you see the Sublician Bridge which formerly [was built] on piles (rested on).
— On the other side of the Tiber the hill (here) nearest is the Capitoline Hill, with the temple of Jupiter Best Greatest on the left, and the Tarpeian Rock on the right.
— Why do they say that the Tarpeian Rock is near the Capitol?

— Because [very famous] men [were carried in triumph to the Capitol] (triumphant on the Capitoline slope climbed), but traitors to the Republic were thrown down from the Tarpeian Rock which is very near.
— Sometimes they were the same people, and the road from honours to execution was short!
— This [great building] (mass) on the right bank of the Tiber, isn't it the Mausoleum of Hadrian?
— Yes, and on the right the Vatican [hill] with the basilica of [Saint] Peter.
— Tomorrow we will visit the Vatican City and perhaps we will see the Sovereign Pontiff.
— Where is the Forum?
— We can't see it, for it is hidden by the Capitol, but from the top of the Capitol [one sees it completely] (far and wide is seen).
— This [railway bridge] that we see to the east, was it destroyed [by an air bombardment] (by aerial bombs)?
— What! You are completely wrong. The day after tomorrow I will give you to read a document on this question.

footnotes: Tiberis, -is, m.; acc. Tiberim; abl. Tiberi. Not to be confused with the emperor Tiberius, -i, Tiberius, who was so unpopular at the end of his reign that his death was greeted with cries of Tiberium in Tiberim (cf. SUETONIUS, De Vita Caesarum, Tib., LXXV).
Medius lacus, the lake of the middle or the middle of the lake. Likewise, in the exercise (P. 15), summo tabulato, the top shelf or the top of the shelf.
Naumachia, -ae, f. (word of Greek origin) [spectacle of] naval combat (machia) (naus = navis), joust. Note the analogy of construction with the Latin naufragium (L. 92, N. 6).
Sublica, -ae, f., pile, stake that one plants in the water.

Jupiter, the greatest of the Olympian gods, has a particular declension: acc. Jovem, gen. Jovis, dat. Jovi, abl. Jove. That of Jesus is much simpler: nom. Jesus, acc. Jesum, and Jesu in the other cases, including the vocative.
Rupes, -is, f., rock, crag; one also says saxum, -i, n.

Proditor, -oris, m., traitor; from prodo, -is, -ere, didi, ditum (pro, do), to produce outside, whence to make known and to betray. Not to be confused with prodeo, -is, -ire, ii, itum (pro, eo), to go forward, to appear (L. 61, P. 13). Note the difference in quantity and accentuation between prōdĕre and prōdīre.
Moles, -is, f.: mass difficult to move or to carry (movere), heap, large structure, war machine; derivative molestus, -a, -um, importunate.

Mausoleum, -i, n., mausoleum, designates a sumptuous funerary monument of great dimensions, such as the one that the widow of King Mausolus offered to her late husband. Hadrian's is also known as the Castel Sant'Angelo.

Basilica, -ae, f., word of Greek origin (basileus, the king): 1° very large buildings serving as tribunal, chamber of commerce, etc.; 2° churches built under the Christian emperors, following the plan of the preceding ones; 3° honorary title granted to certain churches (e.g. the Basilica of Lourdes).
Pyrobolus, -i, m. (pronounced purobolouss); word of Greek origin: pyr (gen. pyros), fire (cf. pyrotechnic); bolos, the dart, what one throws (cf. parabola).
comments: IMPORTANT REMARK: To introduce you to some interesting monuments of ancient Rome without weighing down the text too much, we have taken the liberty, which some will consider abusive, of making ancient monuments and modern monuments coexist. The two texts you will find further on (L. 95 and L. 96) relate to present-day Rome.

Limen, -inis, n., the threshold. — Pessulum, -i, m., bolt. — Sera, -ae, f., the lock; not to be confused with serra, the saw. — Clavis, -is, f., the key. — Compluvium, Impluvium (-ii, n.). — Lacunar, -aris, n., the ceiling (initially, the panels which formed it; from lacuna, -ae, f., hole; itself from locus): false imparisyllabic, like trabs, trabis, f., beam. — Cedrus, -i, f., the cedar; abies, -etis, f., the fir; whence the adjectives of P. 8 and P. 9. Let us note on the same occasion pinus, the pine; platanus, the plane tree; populus, the poplar; pirus, the pear tree, all feminines of the 2nd declension (cf. R. and N. 70). — Caminus, -i, m., fireplace, oven. — Stipes, -itis, m., trunk (separated from its roots), wood for burning (one could have said more simply ligna, pl. of lignum, -i, n., wood). Not to be confused with stirps, stirpis, f., stump (cf. L. 80, N. 9) nor with stips, stipis, f., obol, small coin. — Attingo, -is, -ere, tigi, tactum (from tangere, pft tetigi), to touch.

latin: Placet* domum redire*. Sine eam inspiciamus.
In limine sumus.
Januam aperimus.
Nocte eam pessulo claudimus. Est quoque sera quae clave aperitur.
Per fauces ad atrium pervenimus. Atrium est domi membrum ubi majorem diei partem agimus.
Apud antiquos non erat omni ex parte coopertum.
Per compluvium, non solum aer et lux penetrabant, sed etiam aqua pluvialis, quae in impluvio recipiebatur.
Nostris temporibus, piscina cum piscibus cyprinis sufficit!
Hoc lacunar e cedrinis trabibus conspicuis confectum vere mirabile est.
Non sunt cedrinae trabes, sed abiegnae.
In eodem tabulato sunt culina, triclinium et bibliotheca.
Hoc vaporario hiemali tempore calefimus*.
Est quoque caminus magnus ubi stipites comburi possunt*.
Per gradus ad cubicula ascendamus.
Visne* librum quem in lecto legens somnum facilius capere possis*?
Fac videam istum, in summo tabulato.
Admove sellam vel scabellum cujus auxilio eum attingere possim*.
english: [It is decided] (it pleases) to go back to the house. Let us look at it!
We are on the threshold.
We open the door.
At night we close it with a bolt. There is also a lock which is opened with a key.
By the corridor we arrive [in the living room] (atrium). The atrium is the [room] (member) of the house where we spend the greater part of the day.
Among the Ancients, it was not covered on all sides.
By the compluvium not only the air and the light penetrated, but also the rain water, which was received in the impluvium.
In our time, an aquarium with [red] fish (cyprins) is enough!
This ceiling made of visible cedar beams is truly admirable.
The beams are not of cedar but of fir.
On the same floor, there are the kitchen, the dining room and the library.
With this boiler we are heated [in winter] (by winter time).
There is also a large fireplace where logs can be burnt.
Let's go up to the bedrooms by the stairs!
Do you want a book [to help you fall asleep more easily] (which reading in bed you might more easily take sleep)?
[Let me see] that one, on the top shelf.
Bring a chair or a stool [with the help of which] I might reach it.
